name: UI/UX & Product Design
tagline: Design digital products that are easy, useful and delightful to use.

overview.summary: UX (user experience) designers figure out what people need and how a product should work — through research, user flows, wireframes and usability testing. UI (user interface) designers make it look and feel right — layout, typography, colour, components and interaction. Product designers do both and work closely with product managers and engineers. In 2026, designers are also expected to design AI experiences (chat, agents, generated content) and to use AI tools to prototype faster.
whyTrending: BLS projects web and digital interface designers to grow 6% from 2025 to 2035 with a 2025 US median of $104,000.
AI-powered products need new interaction patterns — conversational interfaces, trust and transparency cues, human review steps — which creates demand for designers who understand AI.
Design systems and accessibility are now standard expectations, and laws such as the European Accessibility Act (applying from June 2025) push companies to fix accessibility.
AI tools (Figma AI features, prototyping assistants) let designers move from idea to working prototype faster, raising the value of designers who can also think in product and code.

roles.title: UX Designer
roles.description: Researches user needs, maps journeys and creates wireframes and prototypes that solve real problems.

roles.title: UI Designer
roles.description: Designs the visual layer: layouts, typography, colour, iconography and component states.

roles.title: Product Designer
roles.description: Owns the end-to-end design of features, from problem framing to high-fidelity design and launch.

roles.title: UX Researcher
roles.description: Plans and runs interviews, usability tests and surveys, and turns findings into design decisions.

roles.title: Design Systems Designer
roles.description: Builds and maintains reusable component libraries, tokens and guidelines shared with engineering.

roles.title: Conversation / AI Experience Designer
roles.description: Designs how users interact with AI assistants and agents, including prompts, errors and trust signals.

beginner: Design principles: hierarchy, contrast, alignment, spacing
Figma fundamentals: frames, auto layout, components
advanced: Product thinking: metrics, prioritisation, business goals
Advanced research: diary studies, A/B tests, quantitative analysis

stack.note: Figma is listed in nearly every UI/UX posting. A strong case-study portfolio matters more than any certificate.

roadmap.title: Design foundations
goals: Learn visual design basics: layout, type, colour, spacing
Recreate 5 screens from apps you admire (pixel-perfect practice)
Read Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics and audit one app
roadmap.milestone: Five polished UI recreations and a written heuristic audit.

roadmap.title: UX process
goals: Interview 5 people about a real problem
Create personas, a journey map and user flows
Wireframe and prototype a solution in Figma
Run usability tests with 5 users and iterate
Check accessibility: contrast, touch targets, focus order
roadmap.milestone: Your first complete UX case study, from research to tested prototype.

roadmap.title: Portfolio and specialisation
goals: Build a small design system with components and tokens
Design one AI-powered feature (e.g. a smart assistant flow)
Learn basic HTML/CSS to collaborate with developers
Publish 2–3 case studies on a portfolio site or Behance
Get feedback from designers on ADPList or local communities
roadmap.milestone: A portfolio with 2–3 strong case studies, ready to send to employers.

projects.title: App redesign with heuristic audit
projects.description: Audit a popular local app (e.g. a transport or utility app) against usability heuristics and redesign three key screens.

projects.title: Landing page for a local business
projects.description: Design a responsive landing page for a café, tuition centre or shop, with mobile and desktop versions.

projects.title: End-to-end UX case study
projects.description: Research a real problem (e.g. finding reliable tutors), interview users, prototype a solution and test it with 5 people.

projects.title: Mini design system
projects.description: Create tokens, typography scale and 15+ components with variants and accessibility notes, documented in Figma.

projects.title: AI assistant experience for a bank or health app
projects.description: Design a trustworthy AI assistant flow — onboarding, conversation, uncertainty states, human handoff and error recovery — and validate it with usability tests.

interview.question: Walk me through your design process.
interview.answer: Understand the problem and users (research), define goals and constraints, explore ideas, prototype, test with real users, iterate, then hand off and measure results after launch.

interview.question: UX vs UI?
interview.answer: UX is how the product works and feels across the whole journey; UI is the visual and interactive layer on screen. Both are needed for a good product.

interview.question: How do you handle feedback you disagree with?
interview.answer: Ask questions to understand the concern, bring evidence (research, data, heuristics), propose testing alternatives, and focus on user and business goals rather than personal taste.

interview.question: How do you design for accessibility?
interview.answer: Follow WCAG: sufficient contrast, readable type, keyboard and screen-reader support, clear focus states, large touch targets, captions and not relying on colour alone.

interview.question: How many users do you need for a usability test?
interview.answer: About five users per round usually reveals most major usability problems; run several small rounds rather than one big one.

interview.question: What is a design system and why use one?
interview.answer: A shared library of components, tokens and guidelines that keeps products consistent, speeds up design and development, and makes accessibility easier to maintain.

interview.question: How do you measure design success?
interview.answer: Define metrics up front — task success, time on task, conversion, retention, support tickets, satisfaction (e.g. SUS) — and compare before and after.

interview.question: How would you design for low-bandwidth users?
interview.answer: Lightweight pages, compressed images, offline states, skeleton loaders, clear retry options and minimal steps to complete key tasks.

interview.question: What makes a good portfolio case study?
interview.answer: A clear problem, your specific role, process with key decisions and trade-offs, evidence from research/testing, final design and measurable outcomes.

interview.question: How do you design AI features users can trust?
interview.answer: Set expectations about what the AI can do, show sources or reasoning where helpful, let users edit/undo, handle uncertainty gracefully and provide a path to a human.

demandNotes.bangladesh: Growing. Software firms, startups, fintech and agencies hire UI/UX designers; many juniors start via freelancing on Fiverr, Upwork or Dribbble.
demandNotes.remote: Good, but portfolio-driven and competitive. Specialising (fintech, SaaS dashboards, AI UX) helps you stand out.
demandNotes.global: High for experienced product designers; entry-level hiring is tighter, so research skills and real case studies are key.
